items.title: Commissioning and market engagement
items.source: Cabinet Office, Sourcing and Consultancy Playbooks and the Procurement Act 2023 guidance
items.body: Commissioning is deciding what outcomes are needed and the best way to achieve them with the money available; procurement is the buying step within it. The cycle is to understand needs, plan, do (buy and deliver) and review. Before a tender, a public body may talk to the market to learn what suppliers can offer and to test whether the requirement is realistic. This must be open and even-handed: the same information goes to everyone, nothing is promised, and what was said is recorded, so that no supplier gains an unfair advantage. Specifications work best when they describe the result needed rather than prescribing exactly how to do it, which leaves room for better ideas.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between commissioning and procurement?

options.text: Commissioning decides the outcomes and how to achieve them; procurement is the buying step
They are two names for the same thing
Commissioning is only for councils and procurement only for central government
Procurement happens first, and commissioning is the contract review

questions.prompt: Why should market engagement before a tender be open and recorded?

options.text: So the winner can be agreed in advance
So no supplier gains an unfair advantage and the process can be defended
Because suppliers are not allowed to ask questions later
To keep competitors from finding out about the tender
It lists every step the supplier must follow
It names the preferred product
It states the results needed and leaves suppliers room to propose how
It is kept as short as possible regardless of detail

questions.prompt: A project manager has had several private conversations with the current supplier about the next tender, and has shared draft requirements only with them. What is the risk and what should happen now?
questions.answer: The incumbent now has an unfair advantage, which breaches equal treatment and risks a challenge. Stop the private contact, tell procurement and legal, share the same information with all suppliers (for example through a published engagement notice), record what was shared, declare any conflict, and let procurement decide whether the competition needs adjusting.
questions.rubric: Should identify unfair advantage / breach of equal treatment and the risk of challenge. Should say to stop, disclose to procurement/legal, level the playing field by sharing the information with all, and keep a record. Credit for noting conflicts of interest.

items.title: The Procurement Act 2023
items.body: The Procurement Act 2023 replaced the Public Contracts Regulations 2015 for procurements started from February 2025 by most public bodies in England, Wales and Northern Ireland (Scotland and devolved Welsh bodies have their own rules). Its objectives are delivering value for money, maximising public benefit, sharing information and acting, and being seen to act, with integrity. Contracts are awarded to the most advantageous tender, which can weigh quality and social value as well as price. Authorities choose a procedure. The open procedure is a single stage in which any interested supplier can bid. The competitive flexible procedure lets the authority design its own process, with stages, shortlists and negotiation, provided it is fair and set out in the tender notice. Notices are published on a central digital platform.

questions.prompt: Which Act replaced the Public Contracts Regulations 2015 for most procurements started in England from February 2025?

options.text: The Public Services (Social Value) Act 2012
The Local Government Act 1972
The Freedom of Information Act 2000
The Procurement Act 2023

questions.prompt: Which is one of the objectives of the Procurement Act 2023?

options.text: Maximising public benefit
Always choosing the lowest price
Keeping all bids secret from the public indefinitely
Giving local suppliers priority in every contract

questions.prompt: Under the Act, how is a contract awarded?

options.text: To the lowest price tender in every case
To the most advantageous tender, weighing quality and social value as well as price
To the first compliant bid received
To the supplier with the largest turnover

questions.prompt: Compare the open procedure with the competitive flexible procedure and say when you might choose each.
questions.answer: The open procedure is one stage: anyone interested can submit a tender, and it fits simple, well-understood requirements. The competitive flexible procedure lets the authority design stages, shortlist, negotiate or run dialogue, so it suits complex or innovative needs. Both must be fair, transparent and follow the process set out in the tender notice.
questions.rubric: Open: single stage, any supplier may bid, suits straightforward needs. Competitive flexible: authority designs its own process (stages, shortlisting, negotiation), suits complex needs; must still be fair and published in the notice.

items.title: Evaluating tenders and awarding the contract
items.body: Evaluation criteria and their weights are published in advance and applied exactly as stated. Evaluators score independently against the published method, record reasons for each score and then moderate together. Anyone with a personal or financial link to a bidder declares it and is usually removed from that part of the evaluation. When a decision is reached, the authority sends bidders an assessment summary and then observes a standstill period before signing; under the Act this is at least eight working days, so a bidder who thinks the process was unfair can challenge before the contract is entered. After signing, a contract details notice is published. Clear records are the best protection against a successful challenge.

questions.prompt: What must be true of tender evaluation criteria?

options.text: They can be changed after bids arrive if the panel agrees
They are kept confidential until the award
They are published in advance and applied exactly as stated
They only need to cover price

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the standstill period after the award decision is notified?

options.text: To let the winning supplier start work early
To allow price negotiations to reopen
To give the authority time to find a new supplier
To give unsuccessful bidders time to challenge before the contract is signed

questions.prompt: An evaluator realises a bidder is run by a close friend. What should they do?

options.text: Declare the conflict at once and follow the procedure for managing or removing them
Score the bid anyway, to stay fair
Say nothing, because the friend's bid may not win
Ask the friend to withdraw

questions.prompt: A losing bidder says your scoring was unclear and threatens to challenge. How do you respond and how could you have reduced the risk?
questions.answer: Give a clear debrief that explains the scores against the published criteria, with the assessment summary and the bidder's strengths and weaknesses. Check the scoring was consistent, the reasons were recorded and the standstill was observed. The risk is reduced by clear criteria, independent scoring, moderated notes, conflict declarations and early legal advice.
questions.rubric: Should include an honest debrief tied to the published criteria, checking consistency, recorded reasons, standstill observed, and legal advice. Should mention preventive steps: clear criteria, independent scoring and moderation, declared conflicts, good records.

items.title: Managing the contract and the supplier
items.source: Cabinet Office, Contract Management Capability guidance; Public Services (Social Value) Act 2012
items.body: Awarding a contract is the start of delivery, not the end. Mobilisation turns the signed contract into a working service. After that, the contract manager tracks performance against the agreed measures, meets the supplier regularly, deals with problems early and keeps a record. Changes to a live contract go through formal change control and must be checked against the rules on modifications, so a small variation does not become an unlawful new award. Social value commitments made in the tender are monitored like any other obligation. Contract reviews ask whether the contract still meets the need, and the options are to extend, re-tender or exit. Exit and transition are planned from the start, so the service continues, data returns safely and the authority is not locked in.

questions.prompt: What is the main job of a contract manager after award?

options.text: To renegotiate price every quarter
To check the supplier delivers what the contract requires and deal with problems early
To wait for the supplier to report problems
To hand all issues to the legal team

questions.prompt: Which Act requires some commissioners to consider economic, social and environmental well-being in their procurement?

options.text: The Equality Act 2010
The Data Protection Act 2018
The Public Services (Social Value) Act 2012
The Localism Act 2011

questions.prompt: How should a change to a live contract be handled?

options.text: By an email between the managers
By waiting until the contract ends
By the supplier deciding the change
Through formal change control, checked against the rules on contract modifications

questions.prompt: A supplier's contract has 12 months left. Describe how you decide between extending, re-tendering or exiting, and what you do about exit planning.
questions.answer: Review performance and value for money, whether the need has changed, what the market now offers and the legal room to extend. Extend only if the contract allows it and it is still good value; otherwise re-tender in good time. Plan exit throughout: return of data, knowledge transfer, continuity of service, staff and asset handover, and who does what.
questions.rubric: Should cover performance review, whether the need and market have changed, legal limits on extension, timing of re-tender, and exit planning (data, continuity, knowledge transfer, handover).
